However, the task (viewing erotic pictures/videos to assess sexual-orientation-related desire) is not clearly described as a social-related task per the listed constructs; abstract insufficient to confirm I1. Include for full-text review to determine whether stimuli/tasks qualify as social processing.
Study is an rsfMRI investigation in prairie voles (non-human animals). It does not involve human participants or task-based fMRI in healthy adults, so it fails inclusion criteria I1 and I2.

fMRI was used to measure neural responses while human participants discriminated affective vocalisations (a social-communication/perception task). The study reports behavioral and neural responses in healthy human participants; no exclusion criteria apply. Thus it meets I1 (social-related fMRI task) and I2 (healthy human participants, adults).

Participants are young children (4 and 6 years old); no adult participants aged 18–65 are included. Therefore the study does not meet inclusion criterion I2 requiring at least one healthy adult group. Abstract provides no evidence of an adult sample, so exclude.

Abstract reports task-based fMRI including social processing and emotion tasks in a large sample from the Human Connectome Project comprised of healthy adult participants, meeting both inclusion criteria. Not a review or meta-analysis. Sufficient information to include for full-text review.

Abstract reports fMRI during social-cognitive tasks (reflection on self and friend’s social attributes) in male adult participants, meeting the review’s focus on social-related processing. Participants are healthy adults (no disorders reported). Not a review/meta-analysis. Thus satisfies I1 and I2.

This is a narrative review/book chapter summarizing behavioral and neuroimaging literature, not an original fMRI study reporting data from participants. It does not describe an fMRI scan of healthy adults performing social tasks, so it does not meet inclusion criteria.

This is a narrative review/book chapter about adolescent social influence and developmental neuroscience; it does not report original fMRI data collected in healthy adults (18–65) and therefore does not meet the review's inclusion criteria.

fMRI study examining perception of social interactions (dyadic interactions vs non-interactive actions), meeting I1. The abstract does not state participant ages or explicit healthy status, so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract; include for full-text review.
Participants are children and adolescents (ages 8–17); no adult (18–65) healthy participant group is reported, so the study does not meet inclusion criterion I2.

This is a review article (Annual Review of Neuroscience) discussing neural mechanisms across primates; the abstract describes synthesis and theory rather than reporting original fMRI data in healthy adult humans. It meets exclusion as a review article.

fMRI study in healthy adult participants performing a social decision-making task (modified prisoner's dilemma) examining social cognition/ToM neural responses. Not a review. Thus meets functional MRI social-task criterion and includes healthy adults.

Abstract reports an independent task-based fMRI study comparing appraisal of social vs. non-social images, matching the review objective of social-related fMRI processing. However, the abstract does not state participant ages or explicitly confirm healthy adult status (18–65); include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Study reports fMRI during an emotion perception task (facial/vocal/bimodal), which is social communication/perception of others (meets I1). The abstract does not specify participant ages or explicitly state they were healthy adults, so include for full-text review to confirm I2.

fMRI was used while healthy human participants made social interaction decisions (free vs. controlled choices), assessing social cognitions and neural correlates of perception/understanding of others; participants described as healthy adults. Not a review.

fMRI study where participants categorized prosodic expressions to infer speakers' communicative intentions (social communication), meeting the social-related task requirement. Abstract does not report participant ages, so inclusion regarding age cannot be fully confirmed from abstract; include for full-text review.

Abstract describes an fMRI study examining agentic self-evaluation and neural correlates (dorsolateral PFC, thalamus), which is social cognition/perception of self—meets I1. The abstract does not specify participant ages or explicitly state healthy adults, so inclusion for full-text review is warranted to confirm I2.

fMRI was used while participants evaluated social attributes of faces (perceived intelligence and friendliness), which is social processing (perception/understanding of others). Participants appear to be healthy adults; no exclusion criteria met in abstract.

Single-case report of an 8-year-old child with massive frontal lesions; not a study of healthy adults (18–65). fMRI was used but not reported as a social-related task in healthy adult participants. Does not meet inclusion criteria I1 or I2.

Participants are children aged 8–12, so the study does not include healthy adult participants aged 18–65 and fails inclusion criterion I2. Although it uses fMRI for social tasks (I1), it does not meet the age requirement for this review.

fMRI study with 34 healthy adult participants performing an empathic accuracy task (continuous rating of others’ emotional states), which is social processing (perception/understanding of others). Participants are healthy adults (within 18–65). Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient detail for inclusion.

The sample comprises adolescent boys (internet-addicted and non-addicted), not healthy adults aged 18–65, so the study does not meet I2 despite using fMRI on social-cognitive tasks (I1). No exclusion criteria (e.g., E1) apply, but absence of an adult healthy group excludes it from the review.

This study used resting-state fMRI (no social-related task) and therefore does not meet inclusion criterion I1. It does include healthy adult controls (I2), but the review requires task-based social processing. Excluded on that basis.
Study uses fMRI in preterm infants (31–36 weeks PMA) studying sensorimotor somatotopy, not social processing and not healthy adults 18–65. Does not meet inclusion criteria I1 or I2.

Title and abstract explicitly report fMRI investigations of social concepts (people and social terms), addressing social processing. Participant health/ages not specified in abstract, so include for full-text to confirm I2.

Abstract reports task-based fMRI including a social cognition task domain, satisfying I1. The abstract does not specify participant health status or ages, so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract alone; include for full-text review to verify healthy adult sample.

Participants are adolescents (ages 14–18). Inclusion criterion I2 requires at least one group of healthy adults aged 18–65. Although the study used an fMRI social-reward task (meets I1), the sample does not meet the adult age range, so exclude.

Task-based fMRI study (double-blind, placebo-controlled) in 55 healthy young men viewing attachment-related erotic and fearful social scenes; directly examines social-related processing in healthy adults.

Event-related fMRI was collected while participants performed a mind-perception task and related social attention was examined, satisfying I1 (social-related fMRI). The abstract does not specify participant ages or explicitly state they were healthy adults, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract; include for full-text review to verify I2.

Study used macaque (non-human primate) subjects for fMRI; does not involve human participants aged 18–65 and therefore does not meet inclusion criteria I1 or I2. Exclude based on participant population mismatch.

This article is a meta-analysis (activation likelihood estimation) of 28 fMRI studies in psychopaths, not a primary fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults. Exclude per E1 (systematic reviews/meta-analyses).

This article is a narrative review summarizing infant fMRI findings and theoretical mechanisms rather than reporting original fMRI data in healthy adult participants. It meets the exclusion criterion for reviews (E1).

Study used fMRI during an emotional face recognition task (processing own child’s facial emotions), a social-processing task. Adult mothers included a healthy control group (mothers without ELM). Thus it meets I1 and I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI task probing recall of relationship episodes (self/others) in 35 healthy individuals—fits social-related processing and fMRI (I1). Age range (18–65) is not reported in the abstract, so inclusion should be confirmed at full-text stage (I2 not verifiable from abstract). Include for full-text review to verify participant ages and other details.

Abstract suggests neural effects of oxytocin on social stimuli (anterior insula) but does not explicitly state fMRI or participant characteristics. Insufficient information to confirm inclusion criteria from abstract alone; include for full-text review.

fMRI study where 16 volunteers viewed and processed verbal and non-verbal social interactions, fulfilling I1. The abstract does not report participant ages or explicitly state healthy adult status, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract alone; include for full-text review.

This article is a review of task-based functional neuroimaging studies in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome rather than an original fMRI study in healthy adults; it meets the exclusion criterion for reviews (E1).

The article is explicitly a review and meta-analysis of social cognition in PTSD rather than an original fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults. It meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews or meta-analyses).

fMRI study where participants evaluated faces varying by race and socioeconomic status (social perception/understanding of others). Sample comprises 61 adult (white male) participants, indicating healthy adult group. Meets criteria I1 and I2 based on abstract information.

Abstract reports an fMRI study of brain responses to faces, voices, and combined emotional expressions—clearly a social perception/understanding of others task. The abstract does not state participant health status or ages (18–65), so include for full-text review to confirm I2.

This is an fMRI study of social processing (learning others' trustworthiness) involving healthy younger and older participants. It meets I1 (social-related task during fMRI) and appears to meet I2 (includes a healthy younger adult group likely within 18–65). No exclusion criteria apply.

The study used fMRI during joint leader–follower interactions (a social-related task) and recruited healthy skilled dancers (adult participants), meeting the review’s focus on social processing in healthy adults. Abstract indicates task-based fMRI and healthy subject groups, so it should be included for full-text review to confirm ages and health details.

The study used resting-state fMRI (rsFC) rather than a task-based fMRI paradigm assessing social-related processing. The review requires functional MRI during a social-related task. Participants are healthy emerging adults (ages ~20–25), so I2 is satisfied but I1 is not.

fMRI study measuring neural representations of others' mental states—clearly a social-related task (Perception and Understanding of Others). Abstract reports human male and female participants but does not specify ages or explicitly state health status, so include for full-text review to confirm criterion I2 (healthy adults 18–65). No exclusion criteria met from abstract.

Study participants are children with NVLD or ASD and typically developing children, not healthy adults aged 18–65, so it fails inclusion criterion I2 (adult healthy sample). The abstract also does not clearly describe task-based fMRI of social processing. Exclude based on participant age/group mismatch.

This is a narrative review of resting-state fMRI findings and manipulations in ASD, not an original fMRI study of social-task performance in healthy adults. It meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses (E1).

Abstract reports fMRI scanning during an iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma (a social decision-making task), satisfying I1. The sample (20 male participants) is described but health status and ages are not explicitly stated in the abstract, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract alone; include for full-text review to confirm participant health/age eligibility.

The study used resting-state fMRI (no task-based social processing) to map a mentalizing network and relies on intraoperative stimulation; it does not report an fMRI scan during a social-related task (fails I1). Participant group appears to be clinical (intraoperative), so healthy adult inclusion is unclear. No systematic review/meta-analysis criteria met.
Study used resting-state fMRI (no social task) and participants are adolescents (mean ~14.5, range 10–18), not healthy adults aged 18–65. Therefore it does not meet I1 or I2.

This article is a multi-method review/meta-analysis synthesizing lesion, TMS, MVPA, and Neurosynth evidence rather than reporting original fMRI scans of healthy adult participants. It meets exclusion criterion E1.

Study used fMRI during a social interaction task (iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma) in healthy subjects randomized to intranasal oxytocin or placebo — meets the review objective. Ages not specified in the abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm age range (18–65).

Abstract reports neural (amygdala/prefrontal) responses to trust-related interpersonal stimuli in BPD versus controls, implying an fMRI social-processing task and inclusion of a healthy control group. The abstract does not explicitly state scanning parameters or participant ages (18–65), so include for full-text review to confirm methods and age range.

Abstract reports an fMRI study in 93 healthy males performing a Taylor aggression paradigm involving social provocation and decisions about retaliatory behavior (social cognition/perception of others). Participants are healthy adults, satisfying inclusion. No exclusion criteria apply.

Abstract describes dual-fMRI hyperscanning while pairs performed an interactive social-exchange task, meeting I1. The abstract does not specify participant ages or that they were healthy adults, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract; include for full-text review to verify I2.

This is an fMRI study using an interpersonal pleasant touch paradigm addressing social reward/processing, and includes a matched non-using healthy control group of adults. Thus it meets I1 (social-related task with fMRI) and I2 (healthy participants aged 18–65 present). Not a review or meta-analysis.

Study used a sample of early adolescents (ages 10.5–13.4), not adults 18–65, and used resting-state fMRI and MRS rather than a task-based social fMRI paradigm. Thus it does not meet inclusion criteria I1 or I2.
fMRI was conducted during spontaneous conversation and repetition tasks (social-related processing), and the study includes an age-matched typically developing healthy control group (young adults).

Abstract reports task-based fMRI during a theory-of-mind (social cognition) task, satisfying I1. Participants are described as younger and older adults but age ranges are not specified, so it is unclear whether a healthy 18–65 group is present; include for full-text review to confirm I2.
This is an animal study using Fmr1 knockout mice and pharmacological intervention; no human participants or human fMRI social-task data are reported, so it fails inclusion criteria I1 and I2.

fMRI was used to identify and modulate a pSTS region responsive to dynamic facial expressions—a social-related task (perception/understanding of others). The abstract does not state participant health status or ages, so inclusion criterion I2 is unclear; include for full-text review to confirm demographics and health.

The study used task-free (resting-state) fMRI rather than an fMRI social-related task, so it does not meet inclusion criterion I1. Although typically-developing controls are present (I2), the absence of a social task excludes it from this review.

fMRI hyperscanning study of live mutual eye contact—a social interaction task—conducted in human adult pairs. The abstract reports task-related neural activation and connectivity during eye contact, meeting the fMRI social-processing requirement. Participants are described as human adults (healthy sample), satisfying the participant age/health criterion.

fMRI study where participants viewed face images and performed perceptual/recognition tasks—fits social processing domain (Perception/Understanding of Others). Participants are human (male and female); abstract does not state ages/health explicitly, so include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Abstract reports task-based fMRI during live reciprocal social interactions (human-human vs human-robot), directly addressing social processing and reporting 21 scanned participants. Participant ages/health status are not specified, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

fMRI was used while participants observed human and robot agents experiencing pain/pleasure, assessing empathy — a social cognitive process. Participants (n=26) were healthy adults. The study meets criteria for social-related fMRI task and includes healthy adult participants. Not a review.

fMRI was used while healthy adult participants watched a narrator using co-speech gestures, addressing social communication and semantic processing in an ecologically valid social interaction. Twenty healthy participants (adults) were tested, satisfying both criteria.

Abstract reports an fMRI study of socioemotional processing (empathy and anxiety), which fits social-related processing (I1). The abstract does not specify participant health status or ages (18–65), so inclusion cannot be confirmed from abstract alone; include for full-text review to assess I2.

Study uses resting-state fMRI rather than a task-based social processing paradigm, so it does not meet I1. Age range is across the lifespan (not specified as 18–65), so I2 is not clearly satisfied. No exclusion criteria (E1) apply.

fMRI study using the Cyberball paradigm (social inclusion) satisfies social-related task requirement. The sample includes a healthy control group (17 HC) alongside clinical groups; participants appear to be adults. Thus I1 and I2 are met based on the abstract.

The study reports fMRI BOLD responses to animacy perception—a basic social-perception process—so it addresses social-related processing (I1). The abstract does not specify participant ages or explicitly state they were healthy adults, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract; include for full-text review to verify eligibility.
This article is a meta-analysis of fMRI studies (not an original fMRI study of participants), meeting the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses.

The study used resting-state fMRI (connectivity at rest) rather than a task-based fMRI during performance of a social-related task, so it does not meet inclusion criterion I1. Participants appear to be healthy adults (N=50).
Participants are children with ASD and age-matched typically developing children (not adults). No group of healthy adults (age 18–65) is included, so study fails inclusion criterion I2.

The study used fMRI while participants played a virtual ball-tossing game inducing social exclusion (a social-related task) and reports neural correlates modulated by social support. The sample comprises 71 healthy female participants. Thus it satisfies I1 (fMRI during a social task) and I2 (healthy participant group).

The study reports fMRI data including social perception and reasoning tasks (social-related processing) performed by 78 individuals, indicating relevant task-based fMRI in humans. No clinical populations are reported, implying healthy adult participants.

fMRI study investigating processing of dynamic facial expressions (social communication/perception) in a participant sample (n=51). Abstract indicates a social-related task and likely healthy adult participants; age range not reported, so full text review is needed to confirm I2. No exclusion criteria met.

fMRI study investigating neural processing of social (dyadic) interactions, satisfying I1. Abstract does not specify participant age range or explicit statement that participants were healthy adults (I2 unclear). Given insufficient participant detail, include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI experiment (N=31) measuring neural responses to disfigured faces—a social perception task (perception/understanding of others). It likely used healthy adult participants, though ages/health not explicitly stated; include for full-text confirmation.

fMRI study using vocal emotional stimuli (social communication/perception) with 36 healthy participants; meets criteria of performing a social-related task (vocal emotion processing) and including healthy adults. Age range not specified in abstract, so included for full-text review.

The abstract describes a review of human neuroimaging literature and theoretical discussion of cerebellar function rather than reporting an original fMRI experiment in healthy adults. It is therefore a review article and meets exclusion criterion E1.

The study used resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) before/after rTMS rather than an fMRI task assessing social-related processing, so it does not meet inclusion criterion I1. Healthy adult participants are included (I2).

The study used resting-state fMRI rather than a task-based social fMRI paradigm, so it does not meet inclusion criterion I1 (fMRI during a social-related task). Although healthy controls were included (I2), the primary imaging was resting-state, so exclude for the review focused on task-based social processing.

The study used rtfMRI neurofeedback for hippocampal self-regulation in healthy volunteers, not a social-related task or paradigm probing social cognition/interaction. Although participants are healthy adults (I2 satisfied), the abstract does not describe any social processing task (I1 not met). No exclusion criteria (e.g., E1) apply.

The study used EEG-fMRI during a color discrimination (visual) task and investigates visual gamma and related networks — not social processing. It does not address social-related constructs (I1 not met). Participants appear healthy but lack of social task means it is irrelevant to the review objective.

The study used fMRI during a social trust task (meets I1) but the healthy control group were adolescents aged 13–19, so they do not meet the required healthy adult age range (18–65) specified in I2. Therefore it should be excluded.

The abstract describes a review/meta-analytic study (combining PubMed literature search, Neurosynth meta-analytic database, and resting-state connectivity analyses) rather than reporting new primary fMRI data from participants. This meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic review or meta-analysis).

The study used fMRI while participants played the prisoners' dilemma (a social/interpersonal decision-making task), and included a healthy control group alongside patients. Thus it satisfies I1 (task during fMRI is social) and I2 (healthy adults included). Not a review article.

Participants are adolescents (age 16–17); inclusion criterion I2 requires at least one group of healthy adults (18–65). Although the fMRI task addresses social-related processing (I1 met), the sample does not include adults, so the study is excluded.

Abstract describes an fMRI study of emotional facial expression processing (a social task), satisfying I1. The abstract does not state whether healthy adult control participants (I2) were included, so inclusion requires full-text review.

The study used resting-state fMRI rather than a task-based fMRI social-processing paradigm. Although behavioral measures of social cognition (emotion/sarcasm recognition) were assessed and a healthy control group was included (I2), the absence of an fMRI social-related task means it does not meet I1.

Abstract reports an fMRI study probing honesty-based trustworthiness impressions and predicting trust behavior, meeting I1. Participant health status and ages (I2) are not specified in the abstract, so inclusion cannot be fully confirmed from abstract alone. Include for full-text review to verify that at least one group are healthy adults (18–65).

The study included only participants with alcohol use disorder (no healthy control group). Inclusion criterion I2 requires at least one group of healthy participants aged 18–65. Although it uses fMRI with emotional face processing (I1), lack of a healthy sample excludes it from the review.

Functional MRI was used while participants observed and discriminated others' hand actions (perception/understanding of others — a social process). The study includes a healthy adult group (n=31). Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient info to meet inclusion criteria.

Abstract reports fMRI during auditory (voice) stimulation addressing voice processing and social cognition, meeting I1. Participant health/age not specified in abstract, so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract alone; include for full-text review to verify participant characteristics.

Study uses multi-voxel pattern analysis of neural representations of social touch (implies fMRI) addressing social processing. Abstract does not clearly state whether a healthy adult control group (age 18–65) was included, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

Abstract reports resting-state fMRI in toddlers with autism (ASD) and an ASD subtype identified by eye-tracking. No task-based social fMRI and participants are not healthy adults (18–65). Does not meet inclusion criteria I1 or I2.

fMRI was used while participants recalled museum displays, and the study addresses collective memory and medial prefrontal cortex involvement in social cognition—meeting I1. The abstract does not specify participant ages or clearly state they are healthy adults (18–65), so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract; include for full-text review to verify participant characteristics.

Abstract clearly states this article is a literature review of hallucinogens and entactogens on social processing; it is a review article, meeting exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews or meta-analyses). No original fMRI experimental data are described in the abstract.

This study is about developmental and sleep questionnaires for ASD screening in children/toddlers and does not report any fMRI data or involve healthy adult participants (age 18–65). It does not meet the review’s fMRI or adult healthy participant criteria.

This is a machine-learning methods paper on probabilistic graphical modeling for multi-view bipartite graph clustering. The abstract does not describe any fMRI data, human participants, or social-related tasks, so it does not meet the review inclusion criteria.

The abstract is a narrative review/perspective of naturalistic fMRI approaches rather than reporting original fMRI data on participants. It summarizes existing findings and methods, meeting the exclusion criterion for reviews/meta-analyses.

This article is a meta-analysis of fMRI studies (systematic synthesis), which meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews or meta-analyses). Excluded based on article type despite relevance to social cognition in healthy adults.

The abstract identifies the paper as a critical appraisal/review of naturalistic stimuli in neuroscience rather than a primary fMRI study. It does not report fMRI data from healthy adult participants. Therefore it meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic review/meta-analysis/review).

Abstract identifies the article as a review (‘The present review’). It is not a primary fMRI study reporting data from healthy adult participants performing social tasks, so it meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews or meta-analyses).

This article is a review of fMRI findings in autism spectrum disorders (a systematic review), not an original fMRI study of healthy adults performing social tasks. It therefore meets the exclusion criterion for reviews/meta-analyses.

Abstract describes an overview/chapter summarizing and summarizing evidence on oxytocin in schizophrenia (a review/narrative chapter), not an original fMRI study. It meets the exclusion criterion for reviews/meta-analyses.

This article is a review/reappraisal of social cognition in multiple sclerosis and discusses neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies rather than reporting an original fMRI experiment in healthy adults. It meets exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses.
Abstract reports an fMRI study probing social reward and threat processing (social-related task) and includes a healthy control group aged 50–60 within the 18–65 range. Thus it meets I1 and I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI task probing social cognition (inferring characters’ mental states from film extracts) and includes healthy control groups. Age range (18–65) not specified in abstract, so full-text review needed to confirm I2. Included for full-text screening.

Abstract reports neural processing of social vs non-social anticipation and feedback in borderline personality disorder, implying a social-related neuroimaging task and likely a healthy control group; however, the modality (fMRI) and explicit mention of healthy participants are not stated. Include for full-text review to confirm fMRI and presence of 18–65 healthy adults.
Abstract explicitly states this article is a review of findings to-date (a review/meta-analysis). It is therefore a systematic review/meta-analysis and meets exclusion criterion E1.

Abstract is a narrative review of neuroimaging findings in autism (discusses multiple imaging modalities and studies in autistic patients) rather than an original fMRI study with healthy adult participants. Therefore it meets the exclusion criterion for reviews/meta-analyses (E1).

This is a narrative review article summarizing social neuroscience in psychiatry rather than an original fMRI study of healthy adults; it meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews or meta-analyses).

This article is a systematic review (title and abstract state this) summarizing trials in schizophrenia, not a primary fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults. It meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic review).

Abstract describes a literature review of fMRI reliability rather than reporting original fMRI data from participants performing a social task. Thus it meets the exclusion criterion for review articles and does not provide primary data on social processing in healthy adults.

This article is described as a mini-review synthesizing MRI and genetic findings (not reporting original fMRI data). It is therefore a review article, meeting exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews or meta-analyses).

This is a narrative review of semantic dementia (neuroimaging, genetics, pathology), not an original fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults. Abstract indicates patient-focused research and does not report healthy adult fMRI social tasks.

Abstract addresses neurobiological correlates of social-cognitive (empathy) alterations in psychopathy, suggesting social-related processing; however it does not explicitly state fMRI methods or presence of healthy control group. Insufficient methodological detail in abstract — include for full-text review to confirm I1 and I2.

This article is a narrative review of eye/gaze processing and neuroimaging findings rather than an original fMRI study with participants performing a social task; it is therefore not eligible (review article).

fMRI study of self–other judgments (social-related processing) meeting I1; includes a typically developing healthy adult control group (age-matched young adults) meeting I2. Abstract provides sufficient detail to include for full-text review.

fMRI study using the Cyberball social inclusion/exclusion paradigm with emotional support in healthy undergraduate participants (n=46), addressing social-related processing (social exclusion and support). Meets inclusion criteria for task and participant population; no exclusion criteria evident from abstract.

The abstract reports fMRI during a dyadic social interaction task in human subjects, directly addressing social processing (I1). The abstract does not specify participant ages or explicitly state they were healthy, so full-text review is needed to confirm I2.

This paper is a coordinate-based Activation Likelihood Estimation meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies, i.e., a meta-analysis rather than an original fMRI study of healthy adults. It therefore meets exclusion criterion E1 (meta-analysis).

Abstract examines motion perception of biological objects (faces), a social-cognition relevant task, and includes an age-matched healthy control group (N=67). However, the abstract does not specify that functional MRI was used. Include for full-text review to confirm I1 (fMRI during a social task).

Abstract reports fMRI studies of theory-of-mind (mentalizing), a social cognitive task, but does not specify whether a healthy adult control group (age 18–65) was included. Insufficient information to determine presence of healthy participants; include for full-text review.

Abstract is a review article synthesizing behavioral and imaging studies of emotion and facial affect in schizophrenia rather than reporting an original fMRI study in healthy adults; therefore it meets the review exclusion (E1).

fMRI BOLD was used while participants performed a socio-emotional face appraisal task (“Do you like this face?”), which is a social-related task. The study includes a healthy control group. Ages not specified in the abstract, so full-text should confirm participants are 18–65.

Abstract explicitly describes a meta-analysis of over 200 fMRI studies. This meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews or meta-analyses), so the study should be excluded based on abstract alone.

This paper is a voxel-based meta-analysis of fMRI studies (a meta-analysis/systematic review), so it meets exclusion criterion E1. Although it concerns fMRI of social/maternal processing, it is not an original empirical fMRI study of healthy adults and therefore should be excluded based on the abstract.

The paper is a multimodal coordinate-based meta-analysis (CBMA) of fMRI and VBM studies of first-degree relatives of schizophrenia patients. As a meta-analysis, it meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic review or meta-analysis) and should be excluded based on the abstract.

The study used fMRI during a task probing understanding of others' regret, which fits social-related processing (perception/understanding of others). The abstract does not report participant ages or explicitly state they were healthy adults, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract. Per screening guidance, include for full-text review to verify participant characteristics.

This is a review chapter summarizing oxytocin effects in ASD (neuroimaging and behavioral evidence), not an original fMRI study reporting task-based social processing in healthy adults. It does not present fMRI data from healthy 18–65 participants and therefore does not meet the review objective.

Abstract lacks detail about task modality and participant groups. Title focuses on schizophrenia and does not state whether an fMRI social-related task was used or whether healthy adult controls (age 18–65) were included. Insufficient information to determine eligibility from abstract alone; include for full-text review.

The study reports an fMRI experiment in which healthy adult participants made self-descriptiveness judgments (social self-processing) while scanned, matching the review objective. It is empirical original research (not a review).

Abstract reports fMRI studies of social perception (visual analysis of others’ actions/intentions) in typically developing adults and developmental work; thus it involves an fMRI social task and includes healthy adult participants. It is a program summary of original fMRI research, not a systematic review/meta-analysis from the abstract.

This article is a review (title and abstract indicate it synthesizes neuroimaging studies) rather than an original fMRI study reporting data; therefore it meets exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews or meta-analyses). The abstract provides no original fMRI data on healthy participants.

Resting-state fMRI in children (ages 7–12) with ASD and typically developing controls; no task-based social processing and no healthy adult (18–65) sample. Therefore it fails inclusion criteria I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria (e.g., E1) apply.
This article is a meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies (title and abstract state meta-analysis) rather than a primary fMRI study of participants. Excluded per E1 (systematic reviews/meta-analyses).

The paper is a narrative review discussing neuroimaging and behavioral studies in high-functioning autism rather than an original fMRI experiment in healthy adults. It therefore meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses and does not provide primary fMRI data on healthy participants.

This study reports resting-state fMRI in children with ASD and typically developing controls (from ABIDE); no task-based social processing fMRI and participants are not healthy adults (18–65). Therefore it does not meet inclusion criteria I1 or I2.

Abstract reports the authors performed three meta-analyses of fMRI studies, i.e., a meta-analysis/systematic review. This meets exclusion criterion E1. Although lesion patient data are included, the primary fMRI component is a meta-analysis rather than original fMRI scanning of healthy adults.

Abstract describes use of functional neuroimaging (simultaneous fMRI of two individuals) to study joint attention and discusses neural substrates of prosocial behavior, indicating task-based fMRI of social processing. Participant health/age not specified; include for full-text review to confirm presence of healthy adult group.

Abstract reports resting-state fMRI in individuals with autism spectrum conditions and does not describe a task-based social processing paradigm. Therefore it does not meet inclusion criterion I1 (task-based social-related fMRI) and is ineligible for this review.
This paper is a large-scale meta-analysis of fMRI studies rather than a primary fMRI study of participants performing social tasks; exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews/meta-analyses) applies.

fMRI was used during a face-encoding task (a social cognition paradigm), and the study included an age- and gender-matched healthy control group. The abstract does not state participant ages (18–65) explicitly, so full-text review is needed to confirm the age criterion.

The study used fMRI while participants performed a social-related task (IAT with faces/names of politicians), examining perception/attitudes toward others. Participants appear to be healthy adults. Fits social processing in healthy adults (I1, I2). Not a review article.

Title and abstract describe an fMRI BOLD response to an 'eyes task' assessing theory of mind/social cognition, meeting I1. The abstract does not specify whether at least one group are healthy adults (18–65), so inclusion for full-text review is needed to determine I2.

Human fMRI study examining mirror neuron responses to hand actions and whether emotional (positive/negative/neutral) cues modulate those responses. The task probes social-cognitive processes (action/emotion perception). Participants are human adults (no clinical groups reported). Thus it meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2.

fMRI was conducted during an empathy-for-pain task (social perception/understanding of others). The study includes healthy young adults aged 20–30 (within 18–65), satisfying I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria are met.

Double-blind randomized crossover fMRI study in 18 healthy right-handed adult males performing a validated Theory of Mind social cognition task (Reading the Mind in the Eyes), meeting social-task and healthy-adult criteria.

The study used fMRI during perception of nonverbal social signals (voice and face), which meets I1 (social-related task). The abstract implies healthy individual subjects but does not explicitly state ages or health status; given ambiguity, include for full-text review to confirm I2 (healthy adults 18–65).

The study used fMRI to examine integration of speaker characteristics with sentence content—an aspect of social communication/pragmatic processing—meeting I1. It includes matched control (healthy) adult participants, meeting I2. No exclusion criteria apply.
This fMRI study scanned healthy adult participants during a social-related task (reflection on self and mother), directly addressing social cognition. It therefore satisfies I1 and I2.

Abstract clearly reports functional MRI recorded during social interactions (dual-fMRI) involving cooperation and competition, meeting I1. The abstract does not explicitly state participant ages or that participants were healthy adults, so include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Participants were adolescents (typically developing and ASD), not adults aged 18–65, so the study does not include a healthy adult group and fails inclusion criterion I2, despite using fMRI and social tasks (I1).

This study used resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) and reports altered default network connectivity and associations with theory-of-mind in schizophrenia; it does not report a task-based social processing fMRI paradigm (I1 not met). It is not a review/meta-analysis. Healthy control inclusion is unclear from the abstract. Exclusion based on failure to meet the task-based inclusion criterion.

This article is a review of seven structural/functional MRI studies in ADHD samples (not primary fMRI research in healthy adults) and thus meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses. It also focuses on ADHD participants rather than healthy 18–65 adults.

Study used fMRI face-processing tasks (meets I1) but participants were individuals with a psychotic disorder only (no healthy adult group reported), so it does not meet I2 (required healthy participants 18–65).

fMRI study examining mentalizing (social cognition) during tasks about self/other; includes an age- and IQ-matched healthy control group of adults. Abstract provides clear evidence meeting inclusion criteria I1 and I2.

Study used fMRI while healthy participants anticipated and interpreted others' actions (badminton stroke direction), fitting 'Perception and Understanding of Others' social processing. Participants are players of varying skill levels (presumably adults). No exclusion criteria met.
This record is a systematic review/meta-analysis protocol rather than an original fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults, so it meets exclusion criterion E1.

The study uses fMRI during an affective mentalizing (social) task (meets I1) but compares psychotic offenders to nonpsychotic offenders drawn from a forensic inpatient population; no group of healthy (community) participants aged 18–65 is described, so it fails inclusion criterion I2.

fMRI was conducted while participants read a suspenseful literary text and rated experienced suspense; reported activation in brain areas associated with social cognition/predictive inference (relevant to perception/understanding of others). The abstract does not state ages explicitly, but participants appear to be healthy adults; include for full-text review to confirm participant age and health status.

The study used fMRI to measure amygdala responses to direct vs. averted gaze (a social-cognition task) in N=55 healthy adult males — satisfying I1 and I2. It is an original experimental study (not a review) and provides sufficient abstract detail for inclusion in full-text review.

fMRI study examining face encoding and recognition (perception/understanding of others), which is a social-related task; includes a healthy adult control group (21 controls). Not a review. Abstract provides clear info matching inclusion criteria.

The study used an fMRI facial emotion recognition task (I1 met) but enrolled only participants with schizophrenia randomized to training or games; no healthy adult control group (age 18–65) is reported, so I2 is not satisfied. Exclude for absence of healthy participants.

The study used fMRI during social-cognition tasks but reports only 13 PTSD patients and does not mention any healthy adult control group; therefore it fails inclusion criterion I2 (no healthy participants aged 18–65).

fMRI study examining cortical processing of vocal (socially relevant) sounds, meeting I1. Abstract does not specify whether a healthy adult control group (age 18–65) was included, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract. Include for full-text review to determine presence of healthy participants and age range.

Abstract reports neural (medial prefrontal) responses to social interaction images, indicating an fMRI social-related task (I1). Although focused on remitted depression, such studies typically include a healthy comparison group; the abstract implies relevance to healthy volunteers but does not explicitly state sample details. Because it likely includes healthy adults and meets the review objective but lacks full participant detail, include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Abstract does not describe any social-related task or social processing; it analyses semi-metric properties of functional brain networks in individuals with familial risk for psychosis versus controls. Therefore it does not meet inclusion criterion I1 (fMRI during a social-related task). No exclusion criteria (E1) apply based on the abstract.
fMRI study where adult participants viewed dynamic emotional facial expressions (a social perception/understanding task), and includes healthy control groups. Thus meets I1 and I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI study of face processing (a social-related task) in adults with Asperger syndrome, meeting I1. The abstract does not state whether a healthy control group (age 18–65) was included, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract. Insufficient information to exclude—include for full-text review to verify presence of healthy participants.

fMRI study where participants viewed cooperative vs. noncooperative interactions (a social cognition/perception task) and includes a healthy matched control group. This meets I1 (social-related fMRI task) and I2 (healthy adult participants). Not a review; no exclusion criteria met.

Participants are children (boys); no healthy adult (age 18–65) group is included. Although the study uses fMRI on social/face processing (I1), it fails inclusion criterion I2 (no healthy adult participants), so it does not meet the meta-analysis population requirement.
fMRI social task is present (I1), but the healthy control group consists of adolescents (ages 12–19), not adults 18–65; thus inclusion criterion I2 is not met. No exclusion criteria (e.g., E1) apply.

The study uses fMRI to investigate memory-retrieval and white-matter connectivity in ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, not social-related processing. It does not meet inclusion criterion I1 (no social task). Participants are unspecified but that is moot given lack of social paradigm.

Abstract reports an fMRI investigation of social cognitive processing and compares patients with schizophrenia to their unaffected siblings, indicating presence of healthy participant group performing social-related tasks. Although ages are not specified, unaffected siblings are likely healthy adults; include for full-text confirmation.

Excluded: all participants were schizophrenia outpatients and no healthy control group (age 18–65) was included, so inclusion criterion I2 is not met. The study does meet I1 (fMRI emotion-recognition task) but lacks healthy participants.

fMRI affective ToM task is social processing (meets I1), but participants are only chronic depression patients with no healthy adult group reported (does not meet I2). Exclude based on absence of healthy participants.

The title indicates a multilevel kernel density fMRI analysis, which is a coordinate-based meta-analysis of fMRI studies rather than a primary fMRI experiment with participants. This meets exclusion criterion E1 (meta-analysis).

fMRI was used while participants performed prayer, which the authors frame as recruiting social-cognition areas (mPFC, TPJ, temporopolar, precuneus), satisfying I1. The sample is described as a group of Danish Christians (healthy adult participants), meeting I2 though exact ages aren’t reported; include for full-text confirmation.

The study reports an fMRI social-contingency task probing self-relevant social reward processing (meets I1) and includes a neurotypical healthy adult control group matched to the ASD group (meets I2). Not a review/meta-analysis. Abstract provides sufficient information to include for full-text data extraction.

The study used resting-state fMRI (no task-based social processing paradigm). Inclusion criterion I1 requires a task-based social-related fMRI. Participants are healthy adults (I2 met), but absence of a social task makes the study ineligible for this review.

The study used near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), not functional MRI; therefore it does not meet inclusion criterion I1. It does include healthy adults (I2), and is not a systematic review (E1 not applicable).

Event-related fMRI using a false-belief paradigm investigated understanding others' mental states (a social cognition task). The abstract implies a sample of individual subjects with personality scores and no indication of clinical populations. Thus it meets I1 and likely I2; include for full-text review to confirm participant ages/health status.

Participants are adolescents (mean ages 15.8 and 16.2), not adults aged 18–65, so the study does not meet inclusion criterion I2. Although it uses fMRI and socioaffective cues (I1), the age criterion excludes it from this review.

Abstract does not state that functional MRI was used, nor does it specify inclusion of healthy adult participants (18–65). Because key inclusion criteria (I1, I2) cannot be confirmed from the abstract, include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

Abstract reports fMRI in first-episode schizophrenia with a healthy control group but does not clearly state that participants performed a social-related task (appears to report intrinsic/background connectivity). Insufficient information to determine whether I1 is met; healthy controls are present (I2). Include for full-text review to confirm task and adult age range.

Randomized, placebo-controlled within-subject fMRI study measuring neural and emotional responses to interpersonal social touch in 40 healthy adult males; clearly a social-related task and includes healthy participants. No exclusion criteria apply.

The study uses resting-state fMRI in an autism clinical context and does not report a task-based social processing paradigm in healthy adults. It therefore fails the required inclusion criteria (I1: task-based social fMRI; I2: healthy adult task group).

Abstract reports an fMRI study of social cognition (fear recognition, theory of mind, gaze processing) in a sample of healthy adult men from the general population; fMRI contrasts and connectivity analyses are reported. This satisfies I1 and I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI study during a face perception task with emotional and neutral stimuli (social-related processing) and explicitly includes a healthy control group compared with social phobia patients. Ages are not specified in the abstract, so full-text should confirm 18–65, but the study meets I1 and I2 based on available information.

fMRI study of altered perception and identification with body checking targets 'Perception and Understanding of Self' (meets I1). Abstract does not specify whether a healthy adult comparison group was included (uncertain for I2), so include for full-text review to determine presence of healthy participants.

fMRI study investigating verbal irony and theory-of-mind processing—clearly a social cognition task (meets I1). Abstract does not specify participant ages or explicitly state groups were healthy adults (I2 unclear), so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

Abstract reports fMRI during a social-related ‘social reflection’ task and includes 22 healthy subjects, satisfying task-based fMRI in healthy participants. Age range not specified in abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm participants are within 18–65.

fMRI study examining perception of vocal emotions (social communication/perception of others) during task; meets social-related task criterion. Abstract does not specify participant ages/health explicitly, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

Participants are children aged 7–12; no group of healthy adults (18–65) is included, so the study does not meet inclusion criterion I2. The study does use fMRI during a social-related movie (I1 satisfied), but absence of adult participants places it outside the review scope.

Participants are described as youth/unaffected youth at familial risk and pediatric bipolar disorder—sample appears to be children/adolescents, not adults 18–65, so inclusion criterion I2 (healthy adults 18–65) is not met. Abstract does not indicate any healthy adult group. No exclusion criteria (e.g., review) apply.

This study used resting-state fMRI in ultra-high-risk (UHR) subjects rather than an active social-related task, and the abstract does not indicate a healthy adult task group (18–65). It therefore fails to meet inclusion criteria I1 and I2.

Abstract explicitly states the article is a review of neuroimaging (fMRI and PET) studies rather than reporting original fMRI data from participants. This meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses (E1).

Abstract describes two fMRI studies in healthy young adults using a social attribution task (perception of human-like interactions), which is a social-related task. The sample includes healthy adults. Not a review or meta-analysis. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2.

fMRI was used while participants made charitable donation decisions (a social-related task involving altruism/moral beliefs), and the study reports healthy adult participants. Thus it satisfies I1 and I2 for inclusion.

This is an fMRI study where mothers were scanned in response to emotional expressions of their own children—a social/attachment-related task satisfying I1. Participants are adult mothers (preterm vs full-term groups) and the abstract does not indicate psychiatric/neurological disorders, satisfying I2 (healthy adult group present). Not a review. Therefore study meets inclusion criteria for social-related fMRI in healthy adults.

Abstract reports neuronal/brain activation (amygdala, STS) related to affective theory-of-mind and emotion/neutral expression processing, indicating fMRI of social-related tasks. However, it focuses on schizophrenia out-patients and does not clearly state whether a healthy control group (age 18–65) was included. Include for full-text review to confirm presence of healthy participants.

Resting-state fMRI study; participants did not perform a social-related task during scanning, so it does not meet inclusion criterion I1. The sample appears to be healthy adults (I2 met), but lack of task-based social processing excludes it from this review.

Event-related fMRI was used during a gaze-processing task probing intentions/social cognition, satisfying I1. A typically developing control group is reported but participant ages are not specified, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract; include for full-text review.

The study used event-related fMRI while participants viewed faces of political candidates—a social perception/affiliation task—and reports healthy adult participants (registered Democrats and Republicans). This satisfies social-related processing (I1) and inclusion of healthy adults (I2).

Abstract reports an fMRI study in which participants performed a virtual-reality social cognition task (attributing others' emotions) and includes a healthy adult control group (n=14), satisfying I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria apply.

fMRI study investigating event simulation and mentalizing-related processes (social cognition) during task performance, meeting the social-related task requirement. The study used resting-state fMRI rather than an active, social-related task, so it does not meet I1. It does include a healthy postpartum control group (I2 satisfied), but the primary inclusion requirement of task-based social processing is not met.

Abstract reports fMRI-based gaze-contingent paradigms that create interactive social stimuli, satisfying I1. Participant health status and ages (I2) are not specified in the abstract, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

Participants are a sample of 17 young adults with high-functioning ASD only; no group of healthy adults is reported, so the study does not meet inclusion criterion I2 (healthy participants aged 18–65).

fMRI was used during a face discrimination task (social processing). The study includes a group of age- and gender-matched healthy adults (chronological age-matched controls), satisfying requirement for healthy participants. Abstract provides sufficient info to meet I1 and I2.

The study uses resting-state fMRI (not a task-based social processing paradigm) and participants are adolescent males (not healthy adults aged 18–65). Therefore it does not meet inclusion criteria I1 or I2. No exclusion criteria (e.g., E1) apply based on the abstract.

Although the study used fMRI to examine pragmatic/social language (meets I1), all participants were children (ASD and typically developing). No healthy adult (age 18–65) group is included, so it fails inclusion criterion I2.

fMRI was used with a social-processing task (direct vs averted gaze across emotions), and the study includes a healthy comparison group (16 healthy adults). Abstract provides sufficient detail to meet inclusion criteria.

Study used fMRI during an affect-matching task with fearful and angry faces (social cue processing), and included a healthy comparison group. Thus it meets the review’s social-processing task requirement and contains at least one healthy adult group suitable for inclusion.

The study used fMRI while participants made emotion (social) and age judgments of faces (social perception of others), and included a healthy community control group of adults. It is an original empirical fMRI study, not a review, meeting inclusion criteria.

Participants are children (children with ASD, unaffected siblings, and matched control children), not healthy adults 18–65, so the study fails inclusion criterion I2. The study does involve an fMRI social task (I1), but the age criterion for the meta-analysis is not met. No exclusion criteria (e.g., E1) apply.

fMRI study investigating neural correlates of promotion/prevention goal activation and self-regulation; task involves social-cognitive processing of personal goals (perception/understanding of self). The study used fMRI during a social-related task (direct vs averted gaze) and included a healthy control group (16 healthy subjects). Age range not specified in abstract, but participants are described as adults; include for full-text to confirm ages and extract data.

fMRI was used to examine neural responses to emotional facial expressions (a social-related task), satisfying I1. The abstract reports WS and control groups, but does not specify that controls are healthy adults aged 18–65, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract. Include for full-text review to verify participant age/health criteria.

Abstract reports an fMRI study of emotional face viewing (social perception), meeting I1. The abstract does not specify participant ages or explicitly state healthy adult sample, so I2 cannot be confirmed from the abstract. No exclusion criteria apply. Include for full-text review to verify participant health/age and other details.

fMRI was used while healthy subjects viewed humorous vs non-humorous cartoons—a task tapping humor/social communication processing, relevant to social-related processing. Abstract confirms healthy adult participants but does not report ages; include for full-text review to verify age range, sample details, and methods.

fMRI study investigating memory for emotional (angry) faces—this is social-related processing (perception/understanding of others). Abstract does not state participant health status or ages, so include for full-text review to confirm healthy adult sample (I2). Not a review/meta-analysis.

Participants are adolescents ('youth'), not adults 18–65, so the study does not meet inclusion criterion I2 (requires healthy participants age 18–65). Although it appears to involve social processing and likely fMRI (VLPFC), the age criterion is not met based on the abstract.

fMRI study measuring mirror neuron system responses during observation of goal-directed hand actions (a social-related task involving perception/understanding of others). Includes a non-alexithymic control group (healthy adults) alongside alexithymic participants. Satisfies I1 and I2.

Abstract reports event-related fMRI during perception of intentional agency from animated shapes, a social-processing task (meets I1). Participant health status and ages (18–65) are not specified in the abstract, so I2 cannot be confirmed; include for full-text review to verify eligibility.

The abstract reports an fMRI study of perception of biological motion, which is a social-cognition-related task (meets I1). Abstract reports an fMRI study examining vicarious somatosensory responses during observation of touch (a social-perception task related to perception/understanding of others) and links results to empathy traits. Abstract explicitly states this is a selective review rather than an original fMRI study. It does not report primary fMRI data on social tasks in healthy adults, so it meets exclusion criterion E1 (review/meta-analysis).

fMRI study where participants observed others’ pain (social perception/understanding of others), and healthy controls are reported (controls compared to patients). Thus it meets I1 and I2 for inclusion.

Abstract is too brief to confirm whether fMRI was conducted during a social-related task or whether healthy adult participants (18–65) were included. No exclusion criteria apply. Include for full-text review to determine I1 and I2.

The study used functional MRI during a social task (modified prisoner’s dilemma) investigating Theory of Mind/representation of others and reports data from healthy control participants (n=20) alongside patients. This satisfies I1 and I2. Not a review/meta-analysis.

Study reports fMRI during a standardized facial emotion recognition task (social communication/perception) in a sample of healthy subjects, meeting both criteria for social-related task and healthy adult participants. Abstract provides sufficient detail to include for full-text data extraction.

fMRI study of social processing (gaze direction) meeting I1. The study includes a typically developing (healthy) comparison group, suggesting I2, though exact ages are not specified; include for full-text review to confirm adult age range.

fMRI study examining perception of self and others (body perception), a social-related task—meets I1. Abstract reports healthy participants but does not state ages (18–65), so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract; include for full-text review to verify age eligibility.

The abstract reports an fMRI study investigating processing of goal-directed actions and inference of others' intentions, which fits social perception/understanding (I1). fMRI was used to measure brain activity during perception of emotional gestures, which is a social-related task (I1). The abstract mentions control participants (healthy), but ages (18–65) are not specified. Insufficient age information; include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Abstract indicates this article is a narrative review of the field (a review of major steps over 3 decades), not an original fMRI study with healthy participants. It therefore meets the exclusion criterion for systematic reviews/meta-analyses (E1).
Abstract explicitly states this is a systematic review/meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies rather than primary fMRI research with participants, so it meets exclusion criterion E1.

This paper is explicitly a systematic review of published neuroscience studies on mirror neurons in autism (title and abstract state it is a systematic review). It is not an original fMRI study of healthy adults, so it meets exclusion criterion E1.

The study used fMRI during a social task (I1 satisfied) but all participants were adolescents (ages 12–18). There is no group of healthy adults aged 18–65, so inclusion criterion I2 is not met. Therefore the study does not match the review’s population.

Abstract describes a review article summarizing neurobiological findings in patients with bipolar disorder rather than reporting a primary fMRI study in healthy adults. It is a secondary review (not original fMRI data) and focuses on patient groups, so exclude.

Abstract describes an fMRI paradigm probing maternal responses to child affect (a social-related task), satisfying I1. Abstract reports fMRI functional connectivity during emotional processing in a sample of 14 females with borderline personality disorder; no healthy control group or adults without psychiatric disorder are mentioned, so inclusion criterion I2 (at least one healthy participant group aged 18–65) is not met. Abstract reports fMRI during a facial imitate/observe task (social processing) and includes people with and without severe mental illness, implying a healthy control group; not a review. Satisfies social-task fMRI and presence of healthy adult participants.

Study examines cognitive deficits in schizophrenia using the MCCB and multimodal imaging in patients, not fMRI of social-related tasks in healthy adults. Does not meet I1 (no social task reported) or I2 (focus on schizophrenia patients rather than healthy 18–65 group).

This is a narrative review of magnetoencephalography (MEG), not an original fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults; does not meet inclusion criteria. It is a review article and not relevant to the meta-analysis objective.

This article is a quantitative meta-analysis of fMRI studies (not a primary fMRI study). Exclusion criterion E1 (systematic reviews or meta-analyses) applies, so it should be excluded despite addressing social/pragmatic language processing in healthy adults.

Study used fMRI during a naturalistic social task (watching sitcom with socially awkward moments) and included a healthy control group, addressing social processing. Age range (18–65) not specified in abstract, so include for full-text confirmation.

Event-related fMRI examined evaluative judgments linked to self-referential processing/theory of mind (a social-related task), and the study included age-matched healthy control subjects (young adults). Thus it meets the fMRI social-task criterion and includes healthy participants.

The study used resting-state fMRI rather than a task-based social processing paradigm, so it does not meet inclusion criterion I1. Although healthy controls were included (I2), the absence of a social-related task makes it ineligible for this review.

fMRI data were acquired while participants played multiple-round trust games (a social interaction/reward task), satisfying I1. The study includes a healthy control group (n=20), satisfying I2. No exclusion criteria are met in the abstract.

Participants are adolescents (study repeatedly states ‘adolescents’), not adults aged 18–65. Although an fMRI social-evaluation task was used (I1) and a healthy control group was included, the sample does not meet the required adult age range (I2), so the study is not eligible for this review.

fMRI responses were measured during passive viewing of natural movies and analyses report voxel tuning differences to a 'social communication' category, indicating social-related processing. Participant health/ages are not specified in the abstract, so full-text review is needed to confirm I2.

Abstract reports an fMRI task probing simulation of others' painful experiences (a social-related process) and includes a psychiatrically-healthy control group. Age range not reported in abstract; include for full-text verification of ages.

Participants are children (typically developing and ASD children), not healthy adults aged 18–65, so inclusion criterion I2 is not met. The study does use fMRI in a social face-processing task (I1), but the age range excludes it from this review.

Abstract does not specify whether fMRI was performed during a social-related task or whether a healthy control group (age 18–65) was included. The study involves oxytocin in adults with autism but provides insufficient details to determine eligibility — include for full-text review.

Title indicates an fMRI study of deception (a social-cognitive process), suggesting I1 may be met. fMRI was used during facial emotion processing (social cognition/perception of others), and the study includes a normal control user group (healthy adults). Thus it meets I1 and I2 and is relevant to social-related processing in healthy adults.

Abstract describes a methodological tutorial on intersubject correlation without reporting an empirical fMRI experiment, participant ages, or social task details. This is a structural MRI volumetric study (manual tracing of fusiform gyrus) in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and controls, not a task-based fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults. It therefore fails I1 (no fMRI social task) and does not meet the review objective.

Does not report an fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults; this is a narrative review proposing BLA deep brain stimulation for severe autism and discusses pathophysiology and a case report. No fMRI task data or healthy adult participant group is described in the abstract.

Participants are adolescents (ages 11.1–15.5), not adults 18–65 required by inclusion criterion I2. The study did use fMRI and a social task (I1 satisfied) but fails the age criterion, so exclude based on population.

Abstract reports an fMRI study of recognition of happy faces (a social cognition task), satisfying I1. Abstract reports an fMRI study examining personal space/affiliation (social vs non-social stimuli) with imaging results; meets I1. The abstract does not explicitly state participant ages or health status, so I2 cannot be confirmed from abstract alone—include for full-text review.

fMRI study where participants viewed social (faces, people) vs nonsocial images, directly addressing social perception (I1). fulltext_screening_results.reason: This is an fMRI study that directly examines social-related processing (perception of others' eye gaze and social attention) using task-based functional MRI in healthy adult participants (n=9, mean age 24). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts to identify face-responsive regions (clusters selected with z>4 and cluster-size thresholds), and provides atlas coordinates and tables/figures of activations using SPM. Thus it meets criteria for using fMRI during a social task (I3), includes healthy adults in the 18–65 range (I4), reports whole-brain group-level task-evoked statistical maps (I5), and provides coordinates/figures as acceptable reporting (I6). No exclusion criteria apply.

The study uses fMRI of social processing (racial ingroup/outgroup face perception) in presumably healthy adult participants, but the full text/abstract does not clearly report a group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map for the healthy/control group. The paper emphasizes an ROI-based analysis of amygdala voxels and does not provide explicit whole-brain voxelwise results or coordinates that can be clearly identified as unmasked healthy-group whole-brain effects. Because inclusion criterion I5 (whole-brain evidence) is not demonstrably met, this study must be excluded per exclusion criterion E2 (studies reporting only ROI analyses with no whole-brain results).

This is an fMRI study that uses social-related tasks (empathic and forgivability judgements), satisfying the review topic. The sample comprises ten volunteers described as study participants (healthy adults), meeting the sample requirement for a healthy adult group. The abstract reports group-level brain activations (e.g., left superior frontal gyrus, orbitofrontal gyrus, precuneus, etc.), indicating whole-brain task-evoked results are reported for the healthy group. Results are described in text/tables (activation loci), so whole-brain evidence is present. Therefore inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6 are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study used event-related fMRI while healthy adult participants (n=16 scanned, 14 included in analysis; ages 18–30) performed a social-evaluative task (trustworthiness judgments vs age judgments). The paper reports group-level, random-effects whole-brain analyses (SPMs), with coordinates and tables of activations (including small-volume corrected results and whole-brain contrasts), and describes task-evoked effects for the healthy control group. Thus it provides whole-brain task activation maps from healthy adults during a social-related task and meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study of social attribution (self-responsibility and self-serving bias) using task-based BOLD fMRI in healthy adult participants (12 neurologically healthy males, ages 20–51). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (SPM99; fixed-effects and follow-up random-effects ROI testing) with results presented as voxelwise statistical maps and coordinate tables. The task is clearly social-related (attribution of positive/negative social events). All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI study of social processing: participants learned moral status (cooperator/defector) via interactive Prisoner’s Dilemma and were scanned while making gender judgments of those faces — a clear social-related task. The sample consists of healthy adults (scanned n=11, ages 21–36). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain random-effects analyses (SPM2) with coordinates and tables/figures of activations. Results are not limited to ROI, connectivity, or between-group contrasts. Therefore it satisfies the review inclusion criteria for task, sample, and whole-brain reporting.

The study reports an fMRI experiment in which healthy adult participants (N=13, mean age 27.2) passively viewed realistic social interaction video clips (a social-related task). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported (corrected P ≤ 0.05 across the whole brain) with figures and tables of activations (including coordinates and clusters), and contrasts versus rest and versus an ‘alone’ condition. These satisfy the review’s requirements for social task fMRI, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain task-evoked results. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, non-empirical, or out-of-range ages) apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants examining processing of mutual vs. averted social gaze (a social-communication/perception task). The sample comprises healthy young adults (reported separately), and the paper reports group-level voxelwise/whole-brain activation maps (t-statistic maps) for the task conditions in the healthy group (in addition to ROI analyses). Thus it meets all required inclusion criteria and violates none of the exclusion criteria.

This study reports an fMRI experiment examining cooperation and competition (social-related processing) in healthy adult participants (ages 21–28). The sample is healthy adults, and group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported (contrasts vs. independent baseline; voxel-level threshold and tables of activations described). Results are presented as between-condition whole-brain contrasts and group SPM analyses. Thus it meets the fMRI social task requirement, healthy adult sample, and provides whole-brain task-evoked group results in standard formats.

This is an fMRI study that implemented a social-related task (evaluative judgments of guilt and embarrassment; Theory of Mind/social cognition), recruited a healthy adult sample (N=19, ages within 18–65), and reported group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise analyses (random-effects contrasts G−N, E−N, G−E, E−G) with coordinate tables and figures. Whole-brain statistical thresholds and extent criteria are described, and regression analyses with group-level maps are reported. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This paper reports two fMRI experiments investigating understanding of intentions in social interaction, demonstrating anterior paracingulate cortex activation. The study addresses social-related processing (theory of mind/social interaction) using task-based fMRI in human participants and reports group-level activation (anterior PCC) consistent with whole-brain task effects. It was published in Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience (2004) and presents empirical fMRI results rather than a review. Therefore it meets the review objective and the inclusion criteria for fMRI social tasks, healthy adult sample reporting, and whole-brain results (reported as activation in anterior PCC). No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical) apply based on the available full-text abstract and bibliographic information.

This is an event-related fMRI study of self-face recognition, which falls under social-related processing (Perception and Understanding of Self). The sample comprises healthy adult participants (10 right-handed adults, mean age 26.9), and results are reported for the healthy group. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (self vs other, other vs self) with cluster-corrected thresholding and tables of MNI coordinates, satisfying whole-brain reporting. Thus all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-healthy-only, or non-empirical) apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study using a social-related task (impression formation about people vs objects) in healthy adults (N=14, ages 18.3–23.7). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise statistical contrasts (e.g., person-impression > other trials) with thresholding (P<0.001) and tables/coordinates for peak activations, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. Results are reported for the healthy sample (no clinical group confound). Thus it meets inclusion criteria for social fMRI in healthy adults and provides whole-brain task-evoked maps/coordinates.

This is an event-related BOLD fMRI study investigating self-face recognition, which is a social-cognitive task addressing 'Perception and Understanding of Self' (social-related processing). The sample consists of 12 healthy adult participants (mean age 19.36), meeting the healthy adult age criterion.
